resource.description: A  mindfulness-based intervention designed to increase metacognitive awareness. It trains the user to stop "fusing" with their emotions and instead observe the causal link between their cognition, emotion, and physical state in real-time.

text.div: Pause for a second! 🛑 Notice your 'Cognitive Triangle' right now: What is one thought you're having, the feeling it's creating, and what your body is doing? Just noticing the link between them is the first step to changing the loop. ✨

resource.description: A Behavioral Activation technique. It targets the "intention-behavior gap" by encouraging a low-barrier physical action to disrupt a negative emotional state, demonstrating that behavior can be a primary driver of mood change.

text.div: Feeling stuck or low? 🔄 Try a 'Triangle Flip': Instead of waiting to feel better to act, change your behavior to shift your mood. Spend 3 minutes tidying your space, stretching, or drinking cold water. Let your actions lead your feelings! 💥

resource.description: A Cognitive Restructuring exercise. It prompts the user to employ "Socratic questioning" to identify cognitive distortions (like all-or-nothing thinking), reducing the emotional intensity of a negative thought by introducing objective evidence.

text.div: Detective Mode: ON! 🔍 Is that negative thought in your head a 100% fact, or just a 'mental filter'? Challenge it: Find one piece of evidence that proves that thought is wrong. Shifting the thought changes the feeling. ⚖️

resource.description: A positive reinforcement and savoring technique. In CBT, it is just as important to map "what works" as it is to fix "what doesn't." This trains the user to recognize the conditions that lead to wellbeing, creating a mental library of success that they can intentionally recreate later.

text.div: Catch a good moment! 🌟 Notice how you're feeling right now. What thought is fueling this positivity, and what action did you take to get here? Save this 'Positive Loop' in your mind—it's your blueprint for when things feel tough. 🔋

resource.title: Catch a good moment! 🌟 Notice how you're feeling right now. What thought is fueling this positivity, and what action did you take to get here? Save this 'Positive Loop' in your mind—it's your blueprint for when things feel tough. 🔋

resource.description: A Value-Alignment technique. It shifts the user's perspective from extrinsic pressure ("I should do this") to intrinsic motivation ("I am doing this because it reflects who I am"), which is a key driver for long-term behavioral change.

text.div: Take a moment to think about your goal for today. Instead of focusing on the effort, ask yourself: Which of my core values does this action support? (e.g., Health, Family, or Growth). Remember that you aren't just 'completing a task'—you are living out what truly matters to you. 🧭

resource.description: An Implementation Intention exercise. It reduces the cognitive load and "decision fatigue" associated with starting a behavior by pre-programming a response to a potential barrier, bridging the gap between intention and action.

text.div: Motivation fades, but a plan stays. 🛠️ Mentally map out your 'Circuit Breaker' for the day: 'IF [this obstacle happens], THEN I will [this small action].' (e.g., 'If I feel too tired to exercise, then I will just do 2 minutes of stretching'). By deciding now, you take the guesswork out of your success. ⚡️

resource.description: A Self-Efficacy building technique. By prompting the user to shrink the goal to a manageable size, it removes the feeling of being overwhelmed and creates a "success experience," which increases the user's confidence to continue.

text.div: If the big goal feels like a mountain right now, stop looking at the peak. 🏔️ Look at your feet. Ask yourself: What is the smallest, easiest version of this goal I can achieve in the next 5 minutes? Commit to that one tiny win. Mastery is built one micro-step at a time. 🏆

resource.description: A Temporal Reframing exercise. It helps the user overcome "present bias" (preferring immediate ease over future gain) by emotionally connecting them to the reward of completion, creating a stronger immediate impulse to act.

text.div: Fast-forward to the end of your day. Imagine you've followed through on your goal. How does your 'Future Self' feel in that moment? 💭 Spend a few seconds really feeling that sense of satisfaction and relief. Now, use that feeling as the fuel to take your first step right now. 🚀

resource.description: An Affect Labeling technique. Research shows that putting feelings into words shifts brain activity from the amygdala (the emotional center) to the prefrontal cortex (the reasoning center), which naturally lowers the intensity of the emotional response.

text.div: Stop for a moment and scan your inner world. 🔍 Instead of saying 'I feel bad,' try to find a precise word for this emotion. Is it frustration? Loneliness? Overwhelm? Or perhaps a mix? Just by naming the emotion accurately, you take the first step in reducing its power over you. 🏷️

resource.description: A Somatic Awareness exercise. By redirecting attention from the narrative of the emotion (the "why") to the physicality of the emotion (the "where"), the user creates a healthy distance (de-centering) and prevents the emotional spiral from escalating.

text.div: Your mind might be racing, but your body is telling the real story. 🌡️ Where is the emotion living in your body right now? Is it a tightness in your chest, a knot in your stomach, or clenched shoulders? Just notice these sensations without trying to change them. Let the feeling be there, and just breathe into it. 🌬️

resource.description: A Functional Analysis of emotion. This encourages the user to view emotions not as "problems to be solved" but as signals of unmet needs. This shifts the user from a state of judgment to a state of curiosity and self-compassion.

text.div: Every strong emotion is a messenger carrying a piece of information. ✉️ Ask yourself: 'What is this emotion trying to tell me I need right now?' Do you need a break? Do you need to feel heard? Or maybe you just need a moment of safety? When you identify the need, the emotion can finally start to soften. 🗝️

resource.description: An Acceptance and Commitment (ACT) technique. Instead of using "avoidance" (which often increases anxiety), this prompts the user to practice radical acceptance. By visualizing the emotion as a temporary wave, the user reduces their struggle against the feeling, which accelerates the natural return to emotional baseline.

text.div: Imagine this emotion is a wave in the ocean. 🌊 You don't have to fight the wave or stop it—you just have to ride it. Remind yourself: 'This is a wave of [emotion], and like all waves, it will reach its peak and then naturally recede.' You are the ocean; the emotion is just the weather. Just keep breathing. 🏄

resource.description: A Behavioral Disruption technique. It explicitly addresses the "depressive spiral" by teaching the user that mood is a result of activity, not a prerequisite for it. This prompts the user to initiate a small "behavioral win" to trigger a shift in emotional state.

text.div: Notice the loop: When mood is low, the urge to withdraw is high. But waiting to 'feel like it' is a trap. 🔄 Try a Spiral Breaker: Choose one tiny activity—even just standing up or opening a window—and do it now. Don't wait for the motivation to arrive; let the action create the motivation. ⚡️

resource.description: A Reward-Based Activation exercise. It helps users categorize activities into "Pleasure" (hedonic reward) and "Mastery" (competence reward). This prevents the frustration that occurs when users try to "force" pleasure during a depressive episode and instead encourages "mastery" as a viable path to mood improvement.

text.div: Not all activities need to be 'fun' to be helpful. ⚖️ Think about your day: Do you need a moment of Pleasure (something that brings joy, like a favorite song) or a moment of Mastery (something that makes you feel capable, like answering one email)? Pick one and commit to just 5 minutes. Which one does your soul need right now? 🌟

Pick one and commit to just 5 minutes. Which one does your soul need right now? 🌟

resource.description: An Opposite Action technique (derived from DBT). It encourages the user to consciously act against a maladaptive emotional urge. This demonstrates the "interconnection of behavior and mood," showing the user that they can influence their internal state by changing their external actions.

text.div: Your mood is currently suggesting 'withdraw' or 'stay still.' What would the Opposite Action be? ↔️ If the urge is to hide, try a brief moment of connection. If the urge is to be silent, try a humming a tune. By acting opposite to the urge, you send a signal to your brain that you are safe and capable. 🚀

resource.description: A Friction Reduction strategy. By focusing on the "entry point" of a behavior rather than the completion of the goal, this reduces the perceived effort and the fear of failure, making it significantly easier for a user in a low-activation state to begin.

text.div: When the mountain looks too high, lower the bar. 📉 Forget the 'whole' activity. Instead, ask yourself: 'What is the absolute easiest first step?' Not 'Clean the kitchen,' but 'Put one dish in the dishwasher.' Just do the first 1% of the task. Once the friction of starting is gone, the rest becomes easier. 🪜

resource.description: A Rapid Vagal Tone exercise. This specific breathing pattern (double-inhale, long-exhale) is one of the fastest ways to trigger the parasympathetic nervous system, lowering the heart rate and signaling to the brain that the immediate "threat" has passed.

text.div: Your nervous system needs a quick reset. 🌬️ Try the 'Physiological Sigh': Take a deep breath in through your nose, and at the very top, take one more tiny sharp inhale to fully inflate your lungs. Now, let out a long, slow exhale through your mouth. Do this twice more. Feel the tension leave your body with the air. 📉

resource.description: A simplified Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) technique. By creating a sharp contrast between extreme tension and complete release, the user becomes more aware of their physiological stress and can physically "force" a state of relaxation.

text.div: Tension often hides where we can't see it. 🧊 Scan your body for 'hidden knots'—your jaw, your shoulders, or your fists. Squeeze them as tight as you possibly can for 5 seconds... and now, let them completely melt. Feel the difference between the tension and the release. Your body is now officially on 'standby' mode. ☁️

resource.description: A Sensory Grounding exercise. This technique disrupts "cognitive looping" (worry or rumination) by forcing the brain to switch from internal distress to external sensory input, effectively pulling the user out of an anxiety spiral.

text.div: When your mind is racing, your senses are your anchor. ⚓️ Gently bring yourself back to the present moment: Notice 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. You are here, you are safe, and you are grounded. 🌿

resource.description: A Consistency and Habit-Formation prompt. This emphasizes the "importance of consistent practice" mentioned in the module description. It prevents the user from only using relaxation as a "crisis tool" and instead encourages it as a preventive mental hygiene practice.

text.div: Relaxation is a skill, not a destination. 🛠️ Just like a muscle, your 'calm response' gets stronger the more you use it. Even if you don't feel stressed right now, take 60 seconds to practice a deep breath. By practicing in the quiet moments, you prepare your brain to stay steady during the storm. 🔋

resource.description: An Avoidance Awareness technique. The first step in exposure therapy is recognizing avoidance as it happens. By labeling the urge to avoid, the user moves from a reactive state to an observant state, creating a window of opportunity to choose a different behavior.

text.div: Notice the 'Invisible Wall.' 🧱 Is there something you're currently avoiding or pushing to 'tomorrow'? That urge to withdraw is your anxiety trying to protect you, but it's also keeping you small. Just identify the avoidance: 'I am avoiding [X] because I feel [Y].' Naming the wall is the first step to climbing over it. 🔍

resource.description: A Safety Behavior Disruption exercise. Safety behaviors (subtle rituals used to reduce anxiety) actually maintain anxiety by preventing the user from learning that they can handle the situation on their own. This prompt encourages "pure" exposure.

text.div: Check your 'Safety Behaviors.' 🛡️ Are you doing something to 'survive' this moment—like checking your phone, staying near the exit, or rehearsing what to say? These safety nets feel helpful, but they tell your brain the situation is dangerous. Try dropping one safety behavior for just 2 minutes. See what happens when you trust yourself instead of the net. ⚖️

resource.description: A Graded Exposure technique. To prevent the user from becoming overwhelmed (which can lead to further avoidance), this prompts them to break a fear down into its smallest possible component. This ensures the experience is challenging but manageable, building a track record of success.

text.div: You don't have to leap into the fire; you just have to touch the spark. 🔥 What is a tiny, 1% version of the challenge you're facing? If the goal is 'Speaking in a meeting,' the micro-challenge is 'Asking one short question.' Commit to that one small step right now. Courage is a muscle—let's give it a light workout. 🏋️

resource.description: A Habituation prompt. The goal of exposure is not to "stop feeling anxious" immediately, but to learn that anxiety is tolerable and eventually decreases on its own. This message encourages the user to stay in the feared situation long enough for the physiological arousal to naturally decline.

text.div: The anxiety you're feeling right now is like a wave. 🌊 It will rise, it will peak, and then—inevitably—it will fall. Instead of trying to push the wave away, just surf it. Remind yourself: 'I am feeling anxiety, and I can handle this feeling until it passes.' Stay in the situation; let the wave wash over you. You are stronger than the tide. 🏄

resource.description: A Sensory Observation technique. By shifting focus from internal dialogue (the "narrative") to external sensory data, the user breaks the cycle of rumination and anchors themselves in the present moment, reducing the intensity of anxiety or depressive spirals.

text.div: Step out of your thoughts and into your senses. ⚓️ For the next 30 seconds, just Observe: What are three sounds you can hear right now? What is the temperature of the air on your skin? Don't analyze them—just notice them like a camera recording a scene. You are here, in this moment. 🌿

resource.description: A Cognitive Defusion exercise. By adding the phrase "I am having a thought that..." the user creates a healthy distance between their identity and their mental state. This implements the "Non-judgmental" skill, preventing the secondary distress that comes from judging one's own emotions.

text.div: Notice a thought or feeling appearing right now. 💭 Instead of labeling it as 'bad,' 'wrong,' or 'annoying,' try to Describe it objectively. Instead of 'I'm failing,' try 'I am having a thought that I am failing.' You aren't the thought; you are the one noticing the thought. Let it be there without judging it. ⚖️

resource.description: A Single-Tasking prompt. This targets the "One-mindfully" skill, which combats the fragmented attention typical of anxiety. It trains the brain to focus on the present task, which reduces cognitive overload and fosters a state of "flow" and calm.

text.div: The world wants you to multitask, but your mind needs a break. 🛑 For the next few minutes, try to be One-mindful: Whatever you are doing right now—drinking water, walking, or typing—do only that. Feel the textures, smell the scents, and give this one activity your full attention. Everything else can wait. 🎯

resource.description: A Participatory Mindfulness technique. While observation is about stepping back, "Participating" is about stepping in. This encourages the user to engage fully with their environment without the interference of self-consciousness, helping them overcome the emotional numbness or detachment often associated with depression.

text.div: Stop observing your life from the sidelines and Participate. 🌊 Whatever you are doing right now, dive into it completely. Throw your whole self into the conversation, the movement, or the breath. Let go of the 'internal critic' and just be a part of the experience. Be 100% present, 100% here. 🌟

resource.description: A Cognitive Mapping exercise. This prompts the user to dissect a stressful moment using the ABC model. By isolating the "Belief" (B) from the "Event" (A), the user realizes they have agency over their emotional reaction by changing their interpretation of the event.

text.div: Pause and look at the chain reaction. ⛓️ A (Activating Event): What just happened? → B (Belief): What did you tell yourself about it? → C (Consequence): How do you feel now? Often, it isn't 'A' that makes us feel 'C', but the story we tell ourselves in 'B'. What a different story would change the feeling? 💭

resource.description: A Cognitive Distortion Identification technique. This trains the user to recognize common biases in real-time. By labeling a thought as a "bias" rather than a "fact," the user creates cognitive distance (defusion) and reduces the emotional impact of the thought.

text.div: Is your mind playing a trick on you? 🃏 Check for a 'Bias': Are you Catastrophizing (predicting the worst), Mind-Reading (assuming you know what others think), or using All-or-Nothing thinking? If you find one, simply label it: 'That's just my [Bias] talking.' Once you name the trick, it loses its power. 🔍

resource.description: A Cognitive Reframing exercise. It teaches the user to distinguish between thoughts that paralyze them (hindering) and thoughts that empower them (facilitating). It encourages the use of a "compassionate observer" perspective to generate more adaptive and helpful cognitions.

text.div: Notice the voice in your head. Is it a Hinderer ('I can't do this') or a Facilitator ('This is hard, but I can handle the first step')? 🔄 Try to flip the script: How would a supportive, wise friend describe this situation to you? Replace the hindering thought with a facilitating one and notice how your energy shifts. ⚡️

resource.description: A Core Belief Intervention. This moves the user from surface-level "automatic thoughts" to deeper "schemas" (core beliefs). By searching for "disconfirming evidence," the user begins to weaken the hold of negative core beliefs and starts building a more adaptive, accurate self-image.

text.div: Listen closely to that recurring negative thought. Is it talking about this one moment, or is it echoing an old belief about yourself (e.g., 'I'm not enough' or 'I'm unsafe')? 🌳 Challenge the root: Is this belief 100% true in every area of your life? Find one piece of evidence from today that proves this old belief is outdated. 🗝️

resource.description: A Problem Discrimination technique. It prevents "cognitive looping" and rumination by helping the user identify when they are trying to "solve" something outside of their control (e.g., other people's opinions), redirecting their energy toward actionable steps.

text.div: Before you dive in, run your problem through the filter: Is this a solvable problem (something I can change) or an unsolvable one (something I must accept)? 🔍 If it's unsolvable, the goal is 'Acceptance.' If it's solvable, the goal is 'Action.' Don't spend 'solving energy' on a situation that only needs 'acceptance energy.' ⚖️

resource.description: A Problem Specification exercise. This is the first step of the 6-step plan. It combats "catastrophizing" by forcing the user to move from an emotional, globalized description of distress to a specific, concrete problem statement.

text.div: A problem well-defined is a problem half-solved. 📝 Stop the mental whirl and define the problem in one clear sentence. Avoid words like 'always' or 'everything.' Instead of 'My life is a mess,' try 'I am struggling to manage my emails this week.' Once the target is small and clear, it becomes a target you can actually hit. 🎯

resource.description: A Divergent Thinking technique. This disrupts the "tunnel vision" that often accompanies anxiety and depression. By encouraging the generation of multiple alternatives without immediate criticism, it lowers the barrier to finding a workable solution.

text.div: Time for a 'Possibility Storm.' ⚡️ Challenge yourself to think of three different ways to handle this situation—including one that feels slightly 'wild' or unrealistic. Don't judge them yet; just list them. By expanding your options, you break the feeling of being 'trapped' and open the door to a solution you might have missed. 🌈

resource.description: An Implementation prompt. This is the final stage of the 6-step plan. It targets the "intention-behavior gap" by reducing the perceived effort of the solution to a trivial level, ensuring the user moves from the planning phase into the action phase.

text.div: The best plan is useless if it feels too big to start. 🪜 Look at your chosen solution and find the 'Nano-Step': the absolute smallest action you can take in the next 10 minutes to get it moving. Not 'Solve the conflict,' but 'Write the first sentence of the text.' Take that one tiny step now and let the momentum do the rest. 🚀

resource.description: A Value-Clarification technique. It prevents "goal fatigue" by reminding the user that the goal is not the end point, but a vehicle for expressing a core value. This reinforces intrinsic motivation and provides a sense of purpose during difficult tasks.

text.div: Take a look at your goal for today. Now ask yourself: How does this specific action serve the person I want to be? 🌉 If your goal is 'Call a friend,' the value might be 'Connection.' When you see the bridge between the chore and the value, the effort feels lighter and the reward feels bigger. 🌟

resource.description: A Goal-Structuring exercise. This prompts the user to apply the SMART framework to a vague intention. By removing ambiguity, it reduces the anxiety associated with "not knowing where to start" and provides a clear binary for success (either it was done or it wasn't).

text.div: Is your goal a 'Wish' or a 'Plan'? 🎯 Turn your intention into a SMART goal: Make it Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Instead of 'I want to be more active,' try 'I will walk for 15 minutes at 5 PM today.' The more precise the target, the easier it is for your brain to hit it. 🛠️

resource.description: A Proactive Coping strategy. This encourages the user to confront potential failures before they happen. By normalizing obstacles and pre-planning "workarounds," the user is less likely to abandon the goal entirely when the first challenge arises.

text.div: Every great goal has a 'But...' 🚧 Look ahead at your plan for tomorrow. What is the most likely thing to get in your way? Now, decide your response: 'If [this obstacle] happens, I will still [do this small part of the goal].' By predicting the storm, you can build the umbrella now. ☔️

resource.description: A Self-Monitoring and Alignment prompt. This prevents "rigid adherence" to a goal that no longer makes sense. It teaches the user that values are the fixed North Star, while goals are flexible paths. This encourages a growth mindset and reduces the guilt associated with "failed" goals.

text.div: Stop for a moment and check your compass. 🧭 Look at your current trajectory: Are your daily actions actually moving you toward your long-term values, or are you just 'staying busy'? It's okay to pivot. If a goal no longer serves your values, give yourself permission to change the goal to fit the value. 🔄

resource.description: An Attention Training technique. Social anxiety is driven by an intense internal focus (self-monitoring). By consciously shifting attention outward to the other person, the user reduces their own anxiety and paradoxically appears more confident and engaged to others.

text.div: Feeling the 'spotlight' on you? 🔦 Remember: Most people are so worried about their own spotlight that they aren't even noticing yours. Try to shift your focus 100% onto the other person. Listen to their words, notice their expression, and be curious about them. When you stop watching yourself, you start connecting. 🤝

resource.description: A Positive Priming exercise. This uses "state-dependent memory" to evoke a feeling of self-efficacy. By anchoring themselves in a past success, the user lowers their baseline anxiety and enters the social interaction with a more adaptive self-image.

text.div: Before you head into your next interaction, find your anchor. ⚓️ Recall a moment when you felt capable, heard, or appreciated in a social setting. Bring that feeling into your body right now. You don't need to be 'perfect' to be valuable; you just need to be present. Carry that version of yourself into the room. 🌟

resource.description: A Skill-Building prompt. This provides a concrete, low-risk tool (open-ended questioning) to improve social fluency. It removes the pressure to be "interesting" and instead focuses on being "interested," which is a key component of social competence and building rapport.

text.div: The secret to great communication isn't knowing what to say—it's knowing how to listen. 👂 In your next conversation, try the 'Curiosity Challenge': Ask one open-ended question (starting with What, How, or Why) based on something the other person just said. Let them be the expert on their own story. 🎯

resource.description: A Cognitive Reframing technique specifically for "Post-Event Processing" (PEP). People with social anxiety often ruminate on their perceived failures after an event, which reinforces avoidance for next time. This prompt interrupts that loop and reinforces a more balanced, adaptive narrative.

text.div: Did you just finish a social interaction? 🛑 Stop the 'Post-Event Review' before it starts. Your brain will try to find everything you did 'wrong.' Instead, force a Positive Filter: Name two things that went okay, or one moment where you were brave. Don't let a 5% awkward moment overshadow a 95% success. ⚖️

resource.description: A Psychoeducational Normalization technique. Shame is a major barrier to treating sexual dysfunction. By reframing a "dysfunction" as a "communication gap" or a "stress response," the user is moved from a state of self-judgment to a state of problem-solving.

text.div: If you're feeling frustration or 'failure' regarding your intimacy, remember: Sexual challenges are more common than the media suggests. 🌸 Instead of labeling it as 'broken,' try seeing it as a communication gap or a physiological response to stress. When we replace shame with curiosity, we create the space needed for healing and exploration. 🗝️

resource.description: An Interpersonal Effectiveness skill. This teaches a specific communication strategy to discuss sensitive topics without triggering defensiveness in a partner. It shifts the dialogue from accusation to request, which is essential for improving sexual satisfaction and emotional intimacy.

text.div: Talking about intimacy can feel daunting. 💬 Try the 'I-Statement' bridge for your next conversation. Instead of 'You don't do X,' try: 'I feel [emotion] when [situation], and I would love it if we could try [action].' Focus on your own needs and desires rather than the other person's shortcomings. It opens the door instead of building a wall. 🚪

resource.description: A Mindful Desire exercise. Many people struggle with sexual dysfunction because they have a narrow definition of intimacy. This prompt encourages the user to expand their "Intimacy Inventory," recognizing that different forms of connection can reduce pressure and actually increase sexual desire.

text.div: Intimacy is more than just the finish line; it's the whole journey. 🕯️ Take a moment to think: What does 'feeling connected' actually look like for you today? Is it a deep conversation, a long hug, or simply sitting in silence together? Identifying your current need for connection helps you ask for exactly what you need. 🌟

resource.description: A Cognitive Reframing technique. This targets "performance anxiety" by challenging the unrealistic standards of sexuality. By promoting the acceptance of imperfection, the user reduces the anxiety that often contributes to sexual dysfunction, allowing for a more relaxed and adaptive experience.

text.div: The 'perfect' experience is a myth created by movies and magazines. 🎬 Real intimacy is often messy, awkward, and imperfect—and that's okay. Can you accept the 'imperfect' moment as a genuine one? By letting go of the pressure to perform, you create the safety needed for real pleasure to emerge. Just be present, not perfect. 🤍

resource.description: A Cognitive Defusion technique. By externalizing the Inner Critic, the user stops identifying with the negative self-talk. This creates a psychological distance that allows them to observe the criticism without being consumed by it.

text.div: Listen closely to your internal dialogue right now. 👂 Is there a voice telling you that you're 'not enough' or 'failing'? Give that voice a name or a character. (e.g., 'The Judge' or 'The Perfectionist'). By naming the Inner Critic, you realize that this voice is just a part of you—it is not the whole truth of who you are. 🔍

resource.description: A Self-Compassion exercise. Most people find it easier to be empathetic toward others than themselves. This prompt uses a "perspective shift" to bypass the Inner Critic and activate the user's capacity for self-kindness and emotional support.

text.div: If a dear friend were in your exact situation right now, what would you say to them? 🤍 You would likely be kind, understanding, and supportive. Now, try saying those exact words to yourself. You deserve the same grace and compassion that you give so freely to others. Let your Benevolent Companion take the lead. 🌟

resource.description: A Resource Activation technique. This focuses on "self-efficacy" and internal strengths. By recalling past success, the user is reminded of their innate capabilities, shifting the focus from perceived deficiencies to existing resources.

text.div: When we feel low, our brain 'hides' our strengths from us. 🙈 Let's bring them back into the light. Think of one thing you have survived, handled, or achieved in the past, no matter how small. What quality did you use to get through it? (e.g., resilience, patience, or courage). That resource is still inside you today. 🔋

resource.description: A Core Belief Intervention. This targets the "conditional self-worth" (the belief that one is only valuable if they achieve certain things). By affirming "unconditional worth," the user builds a stable foundation of self-esteem that is resilient to external failures or internal mood drops.

text.div: Your value is not a variable—it doesn't go up when you succeed or down when you struggle. ⚓️ Remind yourself: 'My worth is constant. It is not defined by my productivity, my mood, or the opinions of others.' Take a deep breath and let that truth settle. You are enough, exactly as you are in this moment. 🤍

resource.description: A Self-Compassion technique. It encourages the user to notice their state without judgment. By validating their exhaustion rather than fighting it, the user reduces the secondary stress of "feeling guilty for being tired," which is often more draining than the fatigue itself.

text.div: Check your internal battery right now. 🔋 Are you running on 10%? Instead of pushing through the exhaustion, try a moment of radical honesty: 'I am tired, and it is okay to be tired.' Acknowledging your limit isn't a failure—it's the first step in recharging. What is one tiny thing you can do right now to give yourself 5% more energy? ☁️

resource.description: A Habit-Formation prompt. It reframes basic hygiene and health habits as acts of self-respect. By labeling them "non-negotiables," it helps the user prioritize basic biological needs, which provides the physiological foundation necessary for psychological work.

text.div: Self-care isn't always a spa day; sometimes it's the boring stuff that keeps us sane. 🛠️ What is one 'Non-Negotiable' for your health today? (e.g., drinking a glass of water, taking your vitamins, or 5 minutes of sunlight). Treat this task as a sacred appointment with yourself. You are worth the effort of your own care. 🌿

resource.description: A Positive Affirmation exercise. This targets the "internalized pressure" that often leads to anxiety. By consciously changing the language from obligation ("should") to entitlement ("deserve"), the user reduces internal conflict and fosters a more supportive relationship with themselves.

text.div: The way you talk to yourself becomes your reality. 💭 Replace one 'I should' with 'I deserve.' Instead of 'I should be more productive,' try: 'I deserve a moment of rest so I can recover.' Feel the shift in your chest as you move from pressure to permission. You are your own most important teammate. 🤍

resource.description: A Somatic Self-Care technique. This uses sensory input to trigger a relaxation response. It teaches the user that self-care doesn't always require a large time investment; "micro-moments" of sensory comfort can effectively lower cortisol levels and provide an immediate emotional reset.

text.div: When the world feels too loud, create a mini-sanctuary for your senses. 🕯️ Take 60 seconds to find one comforting sensory experience: the warmth of a cup of tea, the softness of a sweater, or a scent you love. Let this one small sensation be a signal to your brain that you are safe and cared for. 🌟

resource.description: A Metaphorical Acceptance technique. It illustrates the concept of "experiential avoidance." By visualizing the "dropping of the rope," the user realizes that they don't have to eliminate the emotion to find peace; they simply have to stop the exhausting effort of fighting it.

text.div: Imagine you are in a tug-of-war with a monster, and the rope is your anxiety or sadness. 🧶 The harder you pull to get rid of it, the harder it pulls back. What would happen if you just dropped the rope? The monster is still there, but the struggle is over. For this moment, declare a ceasefire. Stop fighting the feeling and just let it be. 🏳️

resource.description: A Willingness/Expansion exercise. This encourages the user to increase their "psychological flexibility." By treating emotions as temporary guests rather than intruders, the user reduces the fear of the emotion, which paradoxically allows the emotion to pass more quickly.

text.div: Think of your mind as a guest house. 🏠 Right now, a difficult emotion has just checked in. Instead of trying to push the guest out the door, try saying: 'You are unwelcome, but you are allowed to be here.' Make room for the feeling. Notice where it sits in your body. When we stop trying to evict our emotions, they often stop screaming for our attention. 🔑

resource.description: A Dialectical approach (from DBT). This helps the user overcome the "all-or-nothing" thinking that they must feel "good" before they can be "productive." It validates the current emotional state while simultaneously encouraging behavioral action.

text.div: You can feel [Anxious/Sad] AND still take a step forward. ↔️ Acceptance isn't about liking the situation; it's about acknowledging the reality of it. Try this phrase: 'I feel completely overwhelmed, AND I am capable of doing one small thing.' You don't have to wait for the pain to vanish to start living your life. 🌟

resource.description: A Radical Acceptance technique. It uses a nature metaphor to emphasize the impermanence of emotional states. This helps the user detach their identity from their current distress, fostering a sense of stability (the "sky") despite the volatility of their feelings (the "weather").

text.div: Remind yourself: You are the sky, and your emotions are just the weather. ☁️ Some days are sunny, some are stormy, and some are grey. You don't try to 'fix' a rainstorm; you just accept that it is raining. Right now, it is simply [Current Emotion] weather. Let it rain. The sky remains the same, and the weather always changes. 🌈

resource.description: A Behavioral Activation nudge. It targets the physiological interconnection between movement and wellbeing. By prompting a very short "burst" of activity, it lowers the barrier to entry and uses the immediate change in heart rate to disrupt a low-energy or depressive state.

text.div: Your mind and body are a two-way street: when the mind feels stuck, moving the body can 'unlock' the mood. 🔄 Try a Mood-Mover: Just 2 minutes of movement—shake your arms, dance to one song, or walk briskly to the window. Don't wait to feel motivated; use movement to create the motivation. ⚡️

resource.description: A Physiological De-escalation technique. This uses a modified version of progressive muscle relaxation to discharge the physical tension associated with anxiety. It teaches the user to view exercise not as a chore, but as a tool for emotional regulation.

text.div: Stress is a physical energy that gets trapped in your muscles. 🌡️ Give it an exit. Try a Somatic Release: Tense every muscle in your body as hard as you can for 5 seconds, then let go with a loud exhale. Repeat this three times. You aren't just stretching; you're telling your nervous system that the 'fight or flight' energy can finally leave. 🌬️

resource.description: An Environmental Intervention. Based on "Green Exercise" research, this prompt encourages the user to combine physical activity with nature. This synergy is proven to be more effective at reducing rumination and anxiety than indoor exercise alone.

text.div: The world is bigger than the room you're in. 🌿 If you can, step outside for just 5 minutes. Notice the wind on your skin or the color of the trees. Combining movement with nature is a double-win for your brain: it lowers cortisol and pulls you out of your internal loop. Let the environment do some of the work for you. 🌳

resource.description: A Cognitive Reframing of exercise. By shifting the focus from "exercise as a duty" (which can be daunting for those with depression) to "movement as play," it increases the likelihood of adherence and associates physical activity with positive reinforcement rather than effort or failure.

text.div: Exercise doesn't have to be a 'workout'—it can just be joyful motion. 💃 Forget the gym and the calories. What is one way you can move your body right now that feels like play? A stretch, a sway, or a quick walk? Find the movement that feels like a reward, not a task. Your brain loves the play more than the effort. 🌟

resource.description: A Cognitive Offloading technique. This targets "sleep-onset insomnia" caused by rumination. By externalizing the "To-Do" list or worries, the user reduces cognitive arousal, signaling to the brain that it is safe to transition from an active state to a resting state.

text.div: Your brain is trying to 'solve' tomorrow while you're trying to sleep. 🧠 Stop the mental loop with a Brain Dump: Take a piece of paper and write down everything on your mind—tasks, worries, or ideas. Once it's on paper, your brain can stop 'holding' it. Give your mind permission to clock out for the night. 📝

resource.description: A Sleep Hygiene prompt. This addresses the impact of blue light and high-stimulation content on the circadian rhythm. By encouraging a "wind-down" period, it helps the user align their physiological state with their intended sleep schedule.

text.div: Your screen is telling your brain it's still daytime. 🌅 It's time for a Digital Sunset. Put your devices away or switch to 'night mode' now. Replace the scroll with something analog: a book, a stretch, or just a few deep breaths. Give your melatonin a chance to wake up so your mind can finally wind down. 🌙

resource.description: A Somatic Relaxation exercise. This helps users transition from "doing mode" to "being mode." By focusing on the physical sensation of heaviness and release, the user lowers their heart rate and reduces muscle tension, facilitating the onset of the first sleep phase.

text.div: Sleep isn't a switch you flip; it's a slide you glide down. 📉 Let's start the slide with a Body Scan. Starting at your toes, notice any tension and imagine it melting into the mattress. Move slowly up to your calves, knees, hips... all the way to your jaw. As each part relaxes, feel yourself becoming heavier and more still. ☁️

resource.description: A Paradoxical Intention technique. This targets "performance anxiety" around sleep. By shifting the goal from "must sleep" to "just resting," the user reduces the hyper-arousal and frustration that sustain insomnia, often allowing sleep to happen naturally once the pressure is removed.

text.div: Tossing and turning? 🔄 The more you 'try' to sleep, the further it slips away. Stop the struggle. Tell yourself: 'It's okay if I'm not asleep yet. Just resting my body is still valuable.' By removing the pressure to sleep, you lower the anxiety that's keeping you awake. Let the sleep come to you, rather than chasing it. 🤍

coding.display:
The target population consists of adults (typically aged 18–65) who are clinically diagnosed with comorbid anxiety and depressive disorders. While these conditions affect all demographics, there is often a higher prevalence among women and young adults, though the intervention is designed to be inclusive of all genders and age groups.

Regarding technical affinity, the population is characterized as "smartphone-capable." They possess a basic to moderate level of digital literacy, allowing them to navigate a chat-based interface and interact with push notifications. However, it is important to account for "digital fatigue"; because clinical depression can reduce concentration and anxiety can lead to overwhelm, the technical experience must be intuitive, low-friction, and minimally demanding.

The users are typical smartphone owners who are comfortable with app-based communication but may require a supportive, "low-barrier" entry point to ensure that the technology acts as a bridge to recovery rather than an additional source of stress.

The target population consists of clinical patients suffering from comorbid anxiety and depressive disorders, a group characterized by a complex intersection of emotional, cognitive, and physiological dysregulation. Rather than experiencing a single state of distress, these patients often oscillate between states of hyper-arousal (typical of anxiety) and hypo-arousal (typical of depression), creating a volatile internal environment that significantly impairs their daily functioning.

The primary difference between the two conditions lies in how the patient processes stimulation and responds to the environment. Anxiety is fundamentally a disorder of over-stimulation and threat detection. It manifests as a state of heightened vigilance, where the nervous system is primed for danger. This results in somatic reactivity—such as palpitations and tension—and cognitive apprehension, where the mind is preoccupied with worrisome thoughts and the anticipation of future threats. The core struggle for the anxiety patient is the inability to "turn off" the alarm system.

Depression, conversely, is characterized by under-stimulation and motivational deficit. It manifests as a state of emotional and physical withdrawal. The clinical focus here is on negative valence (sadness, guilt, and anger) and anhedonia—the diminished capacity to experience pleasure or reward. While the anxiety patient is "too wired," the depression patient is often "too shut down," struggling with attentional control and a profound lack of positive affect and hope.

For the JITAI, this distinction is critical: the anxiety-driven patient requires tools to de-escalate arousal and ground themselves in safety, while the depression-driven patient requires tools to activate their system and reconnect with reward. The comorbid patient requires a flexible intervention that can distinguish between these two states in real-time, providing somatic calming for anxiety and behavioral activation for depression.

The intervention is a personalized Just-In-Time Adaptive Intervention (JITAI) designed to treat comorbid anxiety and depression. Moving beyond "one-size-fits-all" apps, it uses a self learning algorithms to deliver personalized CBT-based support—such as emotion regulation and behavioral activation—exactly when the user needs it most. 

The system identifies "vulnerability" and "receptivity" states through daily mood assessments (EMA), delivering targeted "micro-interventions" to break negative spirals.
Improvement of depression and anxiety symptoms as measured by the PHQ4.

* If the recent pattern shows clear worsening, acknowledge this gently and encourage using existing support resources in the app or contacting a trusted professional/support person, without sounding alarming.

Task:
Provide one brief, warm, conversational summary of the patient’s trajectory.

* Group Interest/Pleasure and Mood/Hopelessness as “mood and motivation.”
* Group Nervousness/Edge and Worry/Control as “tension and worry.”

* Describe the mid-term pattern based on all available assessments from the last 7 days.
* Describe the long-term pattern based on the full available trajectory.

* Use one reflective sentence that mirrors what the pattern may have felt like.
* If the recent pattern shows clear worsening, acknowledge this gently and encourage using existing support resources in the app or contacting a trusted professional/support person, without sounding alarming.
